title: GTA 6 dazzles gamers in Australia with ‘fully lived-in, breathable world’
content:
Players can renovate houses, fix cars, lift weights and follow the story in Grand Theft Auto VI’s Miami-inspired Vice City

  • Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

    • Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

    Gamers across Australia woke up Thursday morning feeling like Christmas had come early, some bleary-eyed from late-night sessions on the PlayStation, others with grand plans for a weekend foray in Vice City when their day jobs let them loose.

    Grand Theft Auto VI, more than a decade in the making, is here. And the reviews, mere hours into release, reflect universal acclaim. The game has already vaulted to the top spot on Metacritic’s list of the best games of all time, sitting above 1998’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time with an unprecedented 99/100 score.

title: Four Maryland high school students sue after AI mistakes Doritos bag for gun
content:
Football players say they are ‘traumatized’ after being handcuffed and detained by police while waiting for rides home

Four current and former students at a Maryland high school have filed a lawsuit a year after armed police detained them, prompted by an AI alert that mistook a bag of Doritos for a gun, in an incident that left them “fearing for their lives”.

The plaintiffs sued Omnilert, the company behind the AI gun-detection system, Baltimore county police, the board of education, individual officers and the school principal, alleging unlawful detention and search because of technological and human errors.

title: Russian national charged with spying on Silicon Valley tech and defense firm
content:
Igor D’iu is alleged to have unlawfully entered US and reportedly gathered intel about Palantir and its employees

The US Department of Justice has accused a Russian national of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in an alleged effort to gather intelligence for Russia.

On Wednesday, the justice department announced that Igor D’iu had been indicted on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the attorney general, interstate stalking and fraud involving identification documents.

Disruption comes at critical moment, with Grand Theft Auto VI one of the most eagerly anticipated titles in history

The disruption emerged Wednesday, causing frustrated players to flood social media with complaints about failed logins and server connection problems downloading games and updates.

title: Apple outage: iPhone apps suffer disruption days after major Microsoft issues
content:
Google’s Gmail also affected after problems reported in technological infrastructure in the US and worldwide

Thousands reported disruptions to Google’s Gmail and Apple’s iPhone apps, such as Apple Pay and iCloud, on Tuesday, according to Downdetector. Apple confirmed the outages in a statement but said it had resolved them, while Google said it had not seen internal signs of outages.

Apple’s own system status page as of 2.30pmET showed problems with services such as the App Store, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps and AppleCare.

title: Anthropic IPO: how can I buy shares, and is it worth it?
content:
Stock market debut of Claude AI chatbot maker is expected to be one of the biggest flotations in history

The technology company Anthropic is heading for a blockbuster stock market listing this week in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history.

The company is a leader in artificial intelligence, and is best known for its chatbot Claude. The float, which is expected to value the business at $1.4tn (£1tn), comes at a volatile time for tech stocks, yet it has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.

title: Don’t buy new tech this Black Friday: expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops
content:
Tech on its last legs? Refurbished can be the cheaper, greener option. Here’s how to choose well and avoid the pitfalls

• How to make your phone last longer

Even if you do your best to avoid it, it’s hard to escape the noise of retailers offering implausible-seeming Black Friday discounts on desirable technology. What they won’t be so keen to highlight is the huge environmental cost that comes from feeding the capitalist beast year on year, given what an obvious sales vibe-killer it would be.

While the best approach for the planet is to opt out completely and observe the alternative holiday of Buy Nothing Day instead, such an approach can prove self-defeating for your finances in the long term. If you shop smart on Black Friday and avoid the lure of impulse buys, it’s a good time to stock up on the things you need at lower prices than the rest of the year.
snippet:

title: Actors in UK to get more rights over their ‘digital replicas’ in deal on AI protections
content:
Agreement secured by Equity union gives actors rights over payment and consent when digital replicas are used

Actors in the UK are to be given more rights over their “digital replicas” as part of a new agreement on AI protections with TV and film producers, secured after a growing on-set backlash.

Under a wide-ranging new deal secured by Equity, the actors’ union, performers will have the rights to be paid when their digital replicas are used and to consent to whether their digital replica is used or not.
snippet: Agreement secured by Equity union gives actors rights over payment and consent when digital replicas are used

title: Millionaire factory: Anthropic IPO set to fuel AI gold rush in London’s high-end property market
content:
New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores

Sporting hoodies and white trainers rather than the gilets of London’s banker and lawyer class, tech bros can struggle to be taken seriously by the capital’s luxury property agents. “We worked with a young tech entrepreneur with a substantial budget, who agents assumed was looking to rent a one-bedroom flat,” says Jo Eccles, a buying agent who sources off-market properties for ultra-wealthy clients.

But this week’s float by Anthropic, the AI developer behind the chatbot Claude, promises to bring even more credibility for the growing cohort of tech millionaires, which could breathe life into London’s ailing high-end property market. Its IPO on Thursday, expected to value the company at $1.4tn (£1.1tn), is likely to turn more than 4,000 of its staff into millionaires as their stock options vest. SaaStr, a California research firm, has estimated that the minimum value generated for staff at the AI lab will be $20m each.
snippet: New tech wealth, amassed with remarkable speed, is now washing up on British shores
creator: Lauren Almeida
sourceDescription: Technology news, comment and analysis | guardian.co.uk

title: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as a root cause of global outage
content:
Report identifies three factors that led to blackout: a bug, malfunctioning internal connections and server capacity

Microsoft has identified the root causes of the global outage that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software last week.

The office software giant issued an initial report on Monday that identified three factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of its services: a months-old bug, malfunctioning internal connections, and server capacity. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own, but, when taken together, they led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, Microsoft executives said.
snippet: Report identifies three factors that led to blackout: a bug, malfunctioning internal connections and server capacity
creator: Johana Bhuiyan
sourceDescription: Technology news, comment and analysis | guardian.co.uk

title: Ministers to end Palantir’s contract with NHS in England in 2029
content:
DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it

Ministers will end the NHS’s contract with the controversial tech firm Palantir – but not until 2029, to allow time to line up British companies to replace it.

The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has decided to extend Palantir’s contract to provide the federated data platform (FDP) – the software that links different healthcare providers – for two more years rather than exercise a break clause that would have let them axe it next spring.
snippet: DHSC to extend US tech firm’s contract for two more years to allow time to line up British companies to replace it

It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros.

title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
content:
The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country

Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people.
snippet: The privacy issues over the company’s surveillance cameras have caused protests in schools all over the country

title: Farewell, Cybertruck: why the winding down of the ‘Maga hat on wheels’ is a sign of the times
content:
Eccentric and overhyped, Tesla’s Cybertruck became a stand-in for Elon Musk during his ascent in the Republican party. It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse

Three days after a historic blue tsunami changed America’s political landscape, Elon Musk announced Tesla would end production of its hulking Cybertruck next year.

Was it a coincidence? Maybe. Musk said the move was “to make room for increased Cybercab production”, referring to Tesla’s Robotaxi. But the combined circumstances felt highly appropriate: it was the end of an era.

title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
content:
CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.

It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.
snippet: CEO was viewed as ‘irreplaceable’, but recklessness of affair with a woman regarded by US officials as a Chinese spy made him a political liability

title: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
content:
CEO’s affair and resignation has brought company’s murky corporate contracts and supply chains into sharp focus

Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world?

Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run.
snippet: CEO’s affair and resignation has brought company’s murky corporate contracts and supply chains into sharp focus

title: US public workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and some are winning
content:
As governments adopt AI, workers are gaining ground in how it’s used and securing safeguards against its harms

In the shadow of Silicon Valley, workers for the city of Oakland, California, worry the region will deploy AI systems that could increase surveillance and inaccurately evaluate their performance. Pushing for protections to ensure workers won’t be laid off or disciplined by AI, their union overwhelmingly voted on 22 October to authorize a strike, with 94.1% in favor.

“We just want the city administration to really be intentional about how it’s engaging with AI products,” said Julian Ware, an Oakland spatial data administrator and member of International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers Local 21. “Sometimes with a fancy new toy, it actually costs more, it’s more difficult to implement and the results are not as good.”
snippet: As governments adopt AI, workers are gaining ground in how it’s used and securing safeguards against its harms

title: Waymo pulls driverless taxis from freeways across the US after California ban
content:
The autonomous driving company suspended driverless taxi rides on US highways days after California banned the vehicles on its own freeways

Waymo has stopped offering driverless taxi rides on freeways across the US indefinitely. The Alphabet subsidiary pulled its vehicles from highways nationwide after California banned them from freeways in response to recent traffic incidents.

Waymo had allowed riders to hail its robotaxis for freeway rides in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin. The California-based company offers rides on city streets in many other areas, including Las Vegas, Dallas and Denver. Those rides remain unaffected by suspended freeway service.
snippet: The autonomous driving company suspended driverless taxi rides on US highways days after California banned the vehicles on its own freeways

title: Senators criticize Apple and Google for letting teens access ‘nudify’ apps despite parental controls
content:
Exclusive: three Senate Democrats send letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms

A trio of US senators says Apple and Google are failing to effectively detect and remove apps that can be used to generate nonconsensual nude or pornographic imagery. The senators also say Meta is continuing to profit off of ads for these so-called nudification apps that “victimize women and girls worldwide”.

On Wednesday, Ron Wyden, Ed Markey and Ben Luján sent letters to the CEOs of the tech companies, saying the safeguards they have in place to keep nudification off their app stores or platforms are not sufficient.
snippet: Exclusive: three Senate Democrats send letters to tech CEOs saying safeguards against nudification apps are insufficient on their platforms

title: £10m ‘once-in-a-generation’ study to explore effects of children’s social media ban
content:
Research to look at whether ban can make meaningful change in mental health and wellbeing for under-16s

Countries around the world are considering social media bans for children, but whether this would work in practice has been hotly debated. Now researchers are seeking answers through a major scientific study led by Wellcome, which will be the first of its kind.

Ten research projects will explore topics ranging from children’s mental health to their sleep and physical activity, comparing factors before and after the social media ban for children under 16 is introduced in the UK in spring 2027.
snippet: Research to look at whether ban can make meaningful change in mental health and wellbeing for under-16s
creator: Nicola Davis Science correspondent

title: Datacentres to create 70% more carbon emissions by 2030, IEA report warns
content:
Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas

The world’s datacentres will create 70% more carbon emissions within the next four years as the US and China turn to fossil fuels to power their AI growth agendas, according to the world’s energy watchdog.

The International Energy Agency (IEA) warned that datacentres will consume twice as much electricity by 2030 compared with today, with the global expansion of artificial intelligence accounting for three-quarters of this growth.
snippet: Global energy watchdog forecasts huge rise as US and China turn to fossil fuels to power AI growth agendas
creator: Jillian Ambrose Energy correspondent
sourceDescription: Technology news, comment and analysis | guardian.co.uk

title: Anthropic sets share price at $83 for stock market debut, above expected range
content:
Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday

Anthropic set the share price for its debut on the US stock market at $83 on Wednesday, positioning the artificial intelligence company for one of the biggest initial public offerings in history. The firm is slated to begin trading on Thursday under the ticker symbol ANT, with CEO Dario Amodei and other co-founders ringing the bell to open the Nasdaq exchange.

The pricing is above Anthropic’s earlier estimates. Last week, the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, set its preliminary share price at $70 to $78. With all shares counted, those prices put Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) from $1.26tn to $1.41tn. Elon Musk’s SpaceX debuted on Wall Street in June with the biggest market offering ever at $1.77tn. With Anthropic setting its share price at $83, it could now surpass SpaceX.
snippet: Artificial intelligence firm positioned for one of the biggest IPOs in history, with trading slated to begin Thursday
creator: Dara Kerr
sourceDescription: Technology news, comment and analysis | guardian.co.uk

title: From training clips to thirst traps: why athletes are turning to OnlyFans
content:
A professional sports career does not guarantee wealth. And a growing number of athletes are turning to alternative streams of income

“I’m sick and tired of it.” Bart Swings tossed his jacket behind him. It was August 2025, the Winter Olympics were less than six months away, and the Belgian Olympic champion’s injured knee was not getting better. The clip, profanity and all, later ran on the Belgian evening news along with the weather and the football. But the injury update didn’t come from an interview – it was broadcast on the speed skater’s OnlyFans channel.

The subscription site, best known for porn dudes, cam girls and dubiously horny couples, has quietly assembled one of the stranger rosters in professional sport. The list, about 285 athletes deep, includes Olympic speed skaters and rowers, tennis players, surfers and golfers. And, despite its racy reputation, many of the athletes on OnlyFans are not putting out adult content.
snippet: A professional sports career does not guarantee wealth. And a growing number of athletes are turning to alternative streams of income

title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback
content:
After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement

I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.

Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs.
snippet: After refusing to obey the president’s Lake Ontario order, MapQuest briefly rose to No 1 in navigation apps. It’s now a tool in the US anti-surveillance movement

title: ‘My family would kill me if they saw it’: the ‘harmless’ images that can be deadly for women in Pakistan
content:
Tech companies urged to adapt moderation of photos online that can trigger violence against women in some countries

It was just a photo of a smiling girl in jeans and a vest top, the kind of outfit any young woman might wear in any country. But for Maniza*, a teenager from a conservative town in Pakistan who never leaves the house without her hijab, the selfie she took at home put her at very real risk of an “honour” killing.

“My family are really strict and I always wore a hijab. My father didn’t want me to stay in school but my mum pushed him. He said if I got into trouble, he would kill me. It wasn’t just words, he meant it,” she says.
snippet: Tech companies urged to adapt moderation of photos online that can trigger violence against women in some countries

title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?
content:
Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision

For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large.

He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares.
snippet: Huang built Nvidia as a family business but after the co-founder had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, its board faces a difficult decision

title: How GTA started its own moral panic – video
content:
Grand Theft Auto has been so central to the moral panic over graphic video games that some experts have called it the "grand theft fallacy". Nearly 30 years on, that engineered scandal is still bearing fruit.

title: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable
content:
Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller

• This review contains spoilers

Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger.

Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here.
snippet:

title: Are walking pads worth it? We put the best under-desk treadmills to the test
content:
Want to get your steps in while working or watching TV? Our expert puts walking pads through their paces to find the best for comfort, noise and ease of storage

• The best treadmills for your home

You don’t necessarily need to walk 10,000 steps a day to improve your health and wellbeing. In fact, the NHS encourages a slightly more manageable target of just 10 minutes of brisk walking daily to introduce more moderate-intensity physical activity and reduce your risk of early death by up to 15%.

However, even squeezing in “brisk walks” can be a chore, with busy schedules and increasingly desk-bound jobs forcing more of us to remain sedentary for long periods. That is where walking pads come in, being lighter, smaller and often easier to store than bulky and tricky-to-manoeuvre running treadmills.

title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen
content:
Redesigned flagship laptop has a fantastic display, killer performance and the first touchscreen on a Mac, but comes with a serious price tag

Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon.

title: Marlon Brando cool to Jensen Huang joke: how the black leather jacket became a meme
content:
